% conclusion.tex — DisPeD Conclusion Section

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented DisPeD, a two-stage framework that fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-base with a multi-task objective combining 9-class persuasion strategy classification and binary jailbreak-intent classification.
The central result is that persuasion-aware fine-tuning bridges the cross-attack generalization gap that vanilla semantic temporal modeling cannot: DisPeD achieves F1 = 1.000 on unseen Deceptive Delight conversations, a +72 percentage point improvement over vanilla DeBERTa (F1 = 0.284), with zero degradation under adversarial paraphrasing.
Ablation experiments isolate the mechanism behind this gain.
Scrambled persuasion strategy labels reduce OOD F1 by only 1 percentage point, and replacing BiGRU with mean pooling yields identical performance.
These results establish that fine-tuning on persuasion-related text, not specific label assignments or temporal modeling, is the critical ingredient.
The encoder functions as a persuasion-presence detector: exposure to persuasion-domain conversations during multi-task training teaches it to attend to pragmatic cues that transfer across attack families, regardless of supervision quality.
Binary fine-tuning on persuasion-domain text without the strategy classification head also achieves competitive detection performance, confirming that domain exposure drives the generalization gain.
LLM-as-judge baselines confirm the insufficiency of content-level reasoning: GPT-5.5 achieves F1 of only 0.191 to 0.449 on in-distribution Crescendo detection, with 30 to 47\% of responses unparseable.
The 9-class taxonomy is retained not for detection accuracy but for interpretability: distinct attack types produce recognizable persuasion signatures in strategy trajectory analysis that security analysts can inspect without post-hoc explanation methods.

Several limitations constrain the conclusions that can be drawn from this work.
First, the dataset is small: 500 training conversations and 160 OOD test conversations.
These results require validation at larger scale before deployment claims are warranted.
Second, all conversations were generated by Qwen3-8B; real-world multi-turn attacks authored by human adversaries may exhibit different characteristics that our synthetic data does not capture.
Third, DisPeD detects persuasion presence per turn rather than temporal trajectories, so attacks that distribute persuasion sparsely across many turns might evade the detector.
Fourth, TF-IDF achieves F1 = 0.944 on Deceptive Delight, and the gap between DisPeD and bag-of-words narrows when surface features alone suffice; DisPeD's advantage is strongest under adversarial perturbation and for interpretability.
Fifth, only persuasion-mediated attacks fall within scope.
Pure information accumulation attacks, token smuggling, and single-frame roleplay operate through mechanisms orthogonal to persuasion and require different detection approaches.
Future work should evaluate DisPeD on human-generated attack data, scale to larger multi-source datasets that span more attack families, and test robustness against adaptive attacks that target persuasion features directly.
Integration with production safety systems as a complementary multi-turn detection layer is a natural deployment path.

4	\section{Experiments}
5	\label{sec:experiments}
6	
7	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
8	\label{sec:setup}
9	
10	\paragraph{Datasets.}
11	We train on 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak conversations and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, both generated via Qwen3-8B.
12	Topic anchoring ensures that benign conversations cover the same subject domains as jailbreak conversations and controls for topical confounds.
13	For out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, we generate 80 Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024} and 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} conversations through a separate pipeline with no overlap in attack templates or strategies with the training data.
14	The in-distribution (IID) test set consists of 76 held-out Crescendo conversations (38 jailbreak, 38 benign).
15	To assess adversarial robustness, we paraphrase the IID test set to produce 76 perturbed samples with mean BERTScore of 0.92 and lexical overlap of 0.20.
16	
17	\paragraph{Model variants.}
18	We evaluate five variants that share the same Stage-2 pipeline (BiGRU aggregation over DeBERTa [CLS] embeddings, two-layer MLP classifier) and differ only in how the Stage-1 encoder is trained.
19	\textbf{9-class} (full model): DeBERTa-v3-base~\citep{he2021deberta} fine-tuned with a multi-task objective combining 9-class persuasion strategy classification and binary jailbreak-intent classification (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
20	\textbf{Binary}: the 9-class taxonomy collapsed to persuasion-present vs.\ absent, with the same multi-task setup.
21	\textbf{Scrambled}: the full 9-class setup with randomly permuted strategy labels.
22	\textbf{MLM}: continued pretraining with 15\% token masking on the same training conversations, without any classification heads.
23	\textbf{Vanilla DeBERTa}: the unfine-tuned encoder (control).
24	We additionally compare against \textbf{TF-IDF LR} (logistic regression over TF-IDF features) and LLM-as-judge baselines (Section~\ref{sec:llm_judge}).
25	This design progressively strips components to isolate the mechanism: if 9-class $\approx$ binary $\approx$ scrambled, label quality is non-essential; if MLM $\approx$ classification variants, supervised classification itself is non-essential; the gap between any fine-tuned variant and vanilla isolates the contribution of domain exposure.
26	
27	\paragraph{Metrics and implementation.}
28	We report F1 score for binary jailbreak detection at turn prefix lengths $K \in \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$ and on full conversations.
29	IID results for the 9-class and vanilla variants report the mean and standard deviation across three random seeds (42, 123, 456); MLM and other variants use seed 42.
30	Stage-1 fine-tuning uses a learning rate of $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch size 16, and 4 epochs.
31	The multi-task loss weight $\alpha$ is set to 0.3 (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
32	MLM continued pretraining uses the same hyperparameters with 15\% masking probability.
33	Stage-2 classification uses a two-layer MLP trained for 20 epochs.
34	
35	%----------------------------------------------------------------------
36	\subsection{Cross-Attack Generalization}
37	\label{sec:cross_attack}
38	
39	\begin{table*}[t]
40	\centering
41	\small
42	\caption{Cross-attack generalization (F1). All models trained on Crescendo conversations. IID results for 9-class and vanilla report 3-seed mean$\pm$std (seeds 42, 123, 456); all other entries use seed 42. $K$ denotes the number of user turns used for detection. Best per column per section in \textbf{bold}. The MLM variant uses no classification labels yet matches the full 9-class model on OOD Deceptive Delight.}

79	All methods achieve near-perfect F1 on in-distribution Crescendo data.

% Requires: booktabs, multirow, graphicx, multicolumn (standard)

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Datasets.}
We train on 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak conversations and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, both generated via Qwen3-8B.
Topic anchoring ensures that benign conversations cover the same subject domains as jailbreak conversations and controls for topical confounds.
For out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, we generate 80 Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024} and 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} conversations through a separate pipeline with no overlap in attack templates or strategies with the training data.
The in-distribution (IID) test set consists of 76 held-out Crescendo conversations (38 jailbreak, 38 benign).
To assess adversarial robustness, we paraphrase the IID test set to produce 76 perturbed samples with mean BERTScore of 0.92 and lexical overlap of 0.20.

\paragraph{Model variants.}
We evaluate five variants that share the same Stage-2 pipeline (BiGRU aggregation over DeBERTa [CLS] embeddings, two-layer MLP classifier) and differ only in how the Stage-1 encoder is trained.
\textbf{9-class} (full model): DeBERTa-v3-base~\citep{he2021deberta} fine-tuned with a multi-task objective combining 9-class persuasion strategy classification and binary jailbreak-intent classification (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
\textbf{Binary}: the 9-class taxonomy collapsed to persuasion-present vs.\ absent, with the same multi-task setup.
\textbf{Scrambled}: the full 9-class setup with randomly permuted strategy labels.
\textbf{MLM}: continued pretraining with 15\% token masking on the same training conversations, without any classification heads.
\textbf{Vanilla DeBERTa}: the unfine-tuned encoder (control).
We additionally compare against \textbf{TF-IDF LR} (logistic regression over TF-IDF features) and LLM-as-judge baselines (Section~\ref{sec:llm_judge}).
This design progressively strips components to isolate the mechanism: if 9-class $\approx$ binary $\approx$ scrambled, label quality is non-essential; if MLM $\approx$ classification variants, supervised classification itself is non-essential; the gap between any fine-tuned variant and vanilla isolates the contribution of domain exposure.

\paragraph{Metrics and implementation.}
We report F1 score for binary jailbreak detection at turn prefix lengths $K \in \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$ and on full conversations.
IID results for the 9-class and vanilla variants report the mean and standard deviation across three random seeds (42, 123, 456); MLM and other variants use seed 42.
Stage-1 fine-tuning uses a learning rate of $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch size 16, and 4 epochs.
The multi-task loss weight $\alpha$ is set to 0.3 (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
MLM continued pretraining uses the same hyperparameters with 15\% masking probability.
Stage-2 classification uses a two-layer MLP trained for 20 epochs.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Cross-Attack Generalization}
\label{sec:cross_attack}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-attack generalization (F1). All models trained on Crescendo conversations. IID results for 9-class and vanilla report 3-seed mean$\pm$std (seeds 42, 123, 456); all other entries use seed 42. $K$ denotes the number of user turns used for detection. Best per column per section in \textbf{bold}. The MLM variant uses no classification labels yet matches the full 9-class model on OOD Deceptive Delight.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & $K$=1 & $K$=2 & $K$=3 & $K$=5 & Full \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{IID (Crescendo)}} \\[2pt]
9-class (ours) & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} \\
MLM-only & .960 & .974 & .987 & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} \\
Vanilla DeBERTa & .968$\pm$.033 & .978$\pm$.016 & .987$\pm$.000 & .982$\pm$.014 & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} \\
TF-IDF LR & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{OOD (Deceptive Delight)}} \\[2pt]
9-class (ours) & \textbf{1.000} & .990 & .990 & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} \\
MLM-only & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} \\
Vanilla DeBERTa & .575 & .438 & .360 & .311 & .284 \\
TF-IDF LR & -- & -- & -- & -- & .944 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{OOD (FITD)}} \\[2pt]
9-class (ours) & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & -- & -- & \textbf{1.000} \\
Vanilla DeBERTa & .990 & \textbf{1.000} & -- & -- & \textbf{1.000} \\
TF-IDF LR & \textbf{1.000} & -- & -- & -- & \textbf{1.000} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/paper/fig2_cross_attack_bar.pdf}
\caption{Cross-attack generalization at full conversation length. Vanilla DeBERTa collapses on unseen Deceptive Delight (F1 = 0.284) while both the 9-class model and the MLM-only variant achieve F1 = 1.000. TF-IDF LR reaches 0.944 on DD.}
\label{fig:cross_attack}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents F1 scores across three test conditions.
The central finding is that MLM continued pretraining, which uses no classification labels, matches or exceeds the full 9-class model on OOD Deceptive Delight at every prefix length.

\paragraph{IID performance.}
All methods achieve near-perfect F1 on in-distribution Crescendo data.
TF-IDF LR and the 9-class model both reach F1 = 1.000 at every prefix length.
MLM is slightly below at early prefixes (F1 = 0.960 at $K$=1) but reaches 1.000 by $K$=5, and vanilla DeBERTa ranges from 0.968 to 1.000.
The ceiling effect reflects inherent lexical separability between jailbreak and benign conversations: even bag-of-words features suffice when the test distribution matches training.

\paragraph{OOD: Deceptive Delight.}
The DD evaluation reveals the core result.
Vanilla DeBERTa collapses to F1 = 0.284 on full DD conversations despite reaching 1.000 on IID data.
The degradation worsens as more turns are observed (F1 drops from 0.575 at $K$=1 to 0.284 at Full), consistent with the finding that multi-turn attack turns are designed to remain in a ``benign'' embedding region~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}.
The 9-class model maintains F1 $\geq$ 0.990 at every prefix length.
The surprise: the MLM variant achieves F1 = 1.000 at every prefix length on DD, matching or slightly exceeding the 9-class model without any classification supervision.
This result establishes that domain exposure to jailbreak conversation text is sufficient for cross-attack generalization; the classification objective contributes nothing beyond what continued pretraining provides.
TF-IDF LR achieves F1 = 0.944 on full DD conversations, confirming substantial lexical separability even across attack families.

\paragraph{OOD: FITD.}
FITD conversations are easier to detect across all methods.
The 9-class model and vanilla DeBERTa both reach F1 $\geq$ 0.990 at all evaluated prefixes, and TF-IDF LR achieves 1.000 on $K$=1 and full conversations.
The limited differentiation on FITD suggests this attack family shares more surface-level features with the Crescendo training data than DD does.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Decomposing the Detection Mechanism}
\label{sec:decomposition}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Evidence hierarchy on OOD Deceptive Delight. All variants trained on Crescendo and share the same Stage-2 pipeline (BiGRU + MLP). Every variant that includes continued training on jailbreak conversation text achieves DD-Full F1 $\geq$ 0.990; vanilla DeBERTa without continued training collapses to 0.284. MLM continued pretraining without classification labels matches the full model, establishing domain exposure as the mechanism.}
\label{tab:evidence_hierarchy}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & DD-Full & DD-$K$=2 & IID-Full \\
\midrule
9-class (full model) & \textbf{1.000} & .990 & 1.000 \\
MLM-only (no labels) & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & 1.000 \\
Binary (2-class) & .990 & .981 & 1.000 \\
Scrambled labels & .990 & .981 & 1.000 \\
Mean pooling & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & 1.000 \\
\midrule
Vanilla DeBERTa & .284 & .438 & 1.000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

We designed five variants to systematically decompose what enables cross-attack generalization.
Table~\ref{tab:evidence_hierarchy} reports DD and IID F1 for each variant.

\paragraph{Classification supervision is non-essential.}
The MLM variant achieves DD-Full F1 = 1.000 without any classification labels.
This is the definitive test: if unsupervised continued pretraining on the training conversations suffices for OOD generalization, then the classification objective (whether 9-class, binary, or scrambled) cannot be the mechanism.
The evidence hierarchy is clear:
\begin{quote}
\small
vanilla (0.284) $\ll$ MLM (1.000) $=$ scrambled (0.990) $=$ binary (0.990) $=$ 9-class (1.000)
\end{quote}
Every variant that includes continued training on jailbreak conversation text achieves DD-Full F1 $\geq$ 0.990.
The 70+ percentage point gap lies entirely between vanilla and any form of continued training, not between MLM and classification variants.

\paragraph{Label quality and granularity are non-factors.}
Replacing the 9-class taxonomy with randomly scrambled labels reduces DD-Full F1 from 1.000 to 0.990, a gap of 1 percentage point.
Collapsing to binary yields the same 0.990.
Both remain far above vanilla (F1 = 0.284), a gap exceeding 70 percentage points.
These results confirm the domain-exposure interpretation~\citep{gururangan2020dontstop}: the encoder learns useful features from exposure to persuasion-domain text during continued training, regardless of whether the supervision signal is correct, coarse, or random.

\paragraph{Temporal modeling is unnecessary.}
Replacing BiGRU with orderless mean pooling yields DD-Full F1 = 1.000, matching the BiGRU default (Table~\ref{tab:evidence_hierarchy}).
The detection signal resides in individual turn representations rather than their sequential arrangement.
BiGRU is the default aggregator in all other experiments.

\paragraph{Loss weighting is insensitive.}
We evaluated $\alpha \in \{0, 0.3, 0.5, 2.0\}$ for the multi-task loss weight.
All values achieve IID-Full F1 = 1.000.
The $\alpha=0$ variant (persuasion strategy classification only, no intent head) confirms that the persuasion task alone suffices for in-distribution detection.

\paragraph{Ongoing controls.}
Two additional control experiments are in progress to further test the domain-exposure hypothesis.
A topic-classification control replaces the persuasion strategy head with an unrelated classification task on the same training text, testing whether any supervised task on in-domain text suffices.
A Wikipedia-domain MLM control applies continued pretraining on out-of-domain text rather than jailbreak conversations, testing whether the specific text domain matters or whether any continued pretraining is sufficient.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Robustness Under Adversarial Perturbation}
\label{sec:perturbation}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Robustness under adversarial paraphrasing (IID test set, full conversations). Perturbed set preserves semantics (BERTScore 0.92) while altering surface forms (lexical overlap 0.20). $\Delta$: degradation in percentage points.}
\label{tab:perturbation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & Original & Perturbed & $\Delta$ (pp) \\
\midrule
9-class (ours) & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{0.0} \\
Vanilla DeBERTa & 1.000 & .882 & $-$11.8 \\
TF-IDF LR & 1.000 & .987 & $-$1.3 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:perturbation} reports F1 on the original and perturbed IID test sets.
The 9-class model achieves F1 = 1.000 on both, with zero degradation.
Vanilla DeBERTa drops from 1.000 to 0.882 (11.8 percentage points), consistent with its reliance on surface-level features.
TF-IDF LR shows a smaller decline from 1.000 to 0.987 (1.3 percentage points).
Features learned through domain-adaptive continued training capture patterns that are invariant to surface rephrasing, while generic embeddings and lexical features are more sensitive to word-level changes.
MLM perturbation robustness has not yet been tested; the zero-degradation result applies to the classification-based fine-tuning variants.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{LLM-as-Judge Baseline}
\label{sec:llm_judge}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{LLM-as-judge zero-shot Crescendo detection (IID test set). F1 values exclude unparseable responses and therefore represent upper bounds.$^{\dagger}$Unparseable rate increases with context length: 30\% at $K$=2 to 47\% at Full.}
\label{tab:llm_judge}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & $K$=2 & $K$=3 & $K$=5 & Full & Unparse. \\
\midrule
GPT-5.5 & .191 & .273 & .449 & .383 & 30--47\%$^{\dagger}$ \\
Qwen3-8B & .000 & .051 & .146 & .100 & 0\% \\
\midrule
9-class (ours) & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & \textbf{1.000} & 0\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Frontier language models fail at multi-turn jailbreak detection even with full conversation context.
Table~\ref{tab:llm_judge} reports zero-shot performance for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3-8B on the IID Crescendo test set.

GPT-5.5 achieves precision of 1.0 at all turn prefixes but recall ranges from only 0.105 to 0.290, resulting in F1 of 0.191 at $K$=2 and 0.449 at $K$=5.
A substantial fraction of responses are unparseable: the rate increases from 30\% at $K$=2 to 47\% on full conversations.
The F1 values exclude unparseable responses and represent upper bounds.
Full-conversation F1 (0.383) is lower than $K$=5 F1 (0.449) because the unparseable rate grows with context length.
The high precision but low recall pattern suggests that GPT-5.5 is deceived by Crescendo's surface educational framing: the model correctly identifies jailbreaks when it commits to a classification, but the majority of attacks go undetected.

Qwen3-8B performs worse across all prefixes (F1 from 0.000 at $K$=2 to 0.100 on full conversations) and produces no unparseable responses.
The failure of both a frontier commercial model and an open-weight model confirms a fundamental limitation of content-level reasoning for this task.
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo,li2024mhj}, and each turn maintains surface-level coherence with an innocuous cover topic.
Domain-adaptive continued training captures pragmatic features at a fraction of the inference cost of a frontier LLM.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Strategy Trajectory Analysis}
\label{sec:strategy}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/paper/fig3_strategy_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Persuasion strategy transition count matrices for three attack types, based on ground-truth intended strategy labels from the dataset generation pipeline. Color intensity reflects transition count on a symmetric log scale; white cells indicate zero transitions. Crescendo exhibits broad coverage across all strategy categories, while FITD and DD concentrate transitions in smaller subsets. These trajectories are an interpretability contribution: the decomposition in Section~\ref{sec:decomposition} establishes that the taxonomy does not drive detection performance.}
\label{fig:strategy_heatmap}
\end{figure*}

Although the persuasion taxonomy does not contribute to detection performance (Section~\ref{sec:decomposition}), it provides interpretability that MLM-only models cannot offer.
Figure~\ref{fig:strategy_heatmap} shows transition count matrices based on ground-truth intended strategy labels for three attack types.

Crescendo conversations exhibit broad transition coverage across all strategy categories, with 1,818 total transitions.
The highest concentration appears in Role Assignment self-transitions (545), with substantial activity across Emotional Manipulation, Logical Reframing, and Authority Appeal transitions.
This diverse pattern reflects Crescendo's design: each turn draws from a wide repertoire of strategies while incrementally shifting toward more aggressive persuasion.

FITD conversations show a markedly sparser pattern with 541 transitions concentrated in 4 active source strategies.
Role$\to$Obfuscation (161) is the dominant transition, consistent with FITD's structure of securing initial compliance through role assignment before obscuring the escalation path.

DD conversations span 5 active source strategies across 565 transitions.
Emotion$\to$Obfuscation (129) is the dominant transition, consistent with DD's hybrid design of embedding harmful content within emotionally engaging and distracting contexts~\citep{deceptivedelight2024}.

These trajectory signatures allow security analysts to inspect why a conversation was flagged.
Different attack types produce recognizable strategy fingerprints.
This interpretability is the taxonomy's sole contribution after the MLM control result: it does not improve detection, but it makes detection decisions human-readable.
The decomposition in Section~\ref{sec:decomposition} confirms this directly: replacing BiGRU with mean pooling (which discards turn order) yields identical detection performance, so the model detects persuasion presence per turn rather than temporal trajectory patterns.

    Systematic ablation reveals that domain-adaptive continued pretraining on
    jailbreak conversation text (even MLM without classification labels) bridges
    the entire +72pp OOD gap (vanilla F1=0.28 → MLM F1=1.0). Classification
    supervision, label quality, label granularity, temporal modeling, and loss
    weighting are all non-factors. The persuasion taxonomy's sole surviving
    value is interpretability via strategy trajectory analysis.

      - "Surprise finding: MLM continued pretraining on jailbreak conversation text (no classification labels) bridges the entire +72pp OOD gap (F1=1.0)"
      - "Evidence hierarchy: vanilla (0.28) < MLM-only (1.0) = scrambled (0.99) = binary (0.99) = 9-class (1.0)"

      - "Evidence hierarchy: vanilla (0.28) < MLM-only (1.0) = scrambled (0.99) = binary (0.99) = 9-class (1.0)"

You are rewriting the Method section of a paper titled "What Makes Multi-Turn Jailbreaks Detectable? Domain Exposure Bridges the Cross-Attack Gap" for EMNLP 2026.

The original paper framed persuasion-aware classification as the key mechanism for cross-attack generalization. An MLM control experiment (plan_017) **falsified** this claim: continued pretraining with 15% token masking on the same training conversations (no classification labels at all) achieves F1=1.000 on unseen Deceptive Delight, matching the full 9-class model. The paper is now an **empirical findings paper** about what makes multi-turn jailbreaks detectable.

**New core claim**: Domain-adaptive continued pretraining on jailbreak conversation text (even MLM without labels) bridges the entire +72pp OOD gap (vanilla F1=0.28 → MLM F1=1.0). Classification supervision, label quality, label granularity, and temporal modeling are all non-factors. The persuasion taxonomy's sole surviving value is interpretability.

Rewrite `/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_2/projects/persuasion_turn_jailbreak_detect/docs/paper/method.tex` with the following structure (word budget: ~1400 words):

### Structure

**Section 3: Method**

Opening paragraph: DisPeD is a two-stage framework. Stage 1 adapts a turn-level encoder through continued training on jailbreak conversation text. Stage 2 aggregates turn representations for conversation-level classification. We design five Stage-1 variants to systematically decompose what enables cross-attack generalization. Figure 1 shows the pipeline.

**3.1 Problem Formulation** — Keep as-is (binary classification over user turn prefixes, K-prefix formulation, rationale for user-turns-only). This subsection is fine.

**3.2 Stage 1: Turn-Level Encoder Adaptation** — This is the key rewrite. Frame as "ablation-centric design" rather than "persuasion-aware fine-tuning is the mechanism". Describe ALL 5 variants:

1. **9-class (full model)**: DeBERTa-v3-base fine-tuned with multi-task objective: 9-class persuasion strategy classification + binary jailbreak-intent classification. Loss: L = L_strategy + α·L_intent, α=0.3. [CLS] token as turn representation.

2. **Binary**: Same multi-task setup but 9-class collapsed to persuasion-present/absent (2-class). Tests whether label granularity matters.

3. **Scrambled**: Full 9-class setup with randomly permuted strategy labels. Tests whether label correctness matters.

4. **MLM-only**: Continued pretraining with 15% token masking on the same training conversations. No classification heads. Tests whether supervised classification is necessary at all.

5. **Vanilla DeBERTa**: Unfine-tuned pretrained encoder. Control baseline.

Explain the logic: these five variants form a systematic decomposition. If 9-class ≈ binary ≈ scrambled, label quality/granularity are non-essential. If MLM ≈ classification variants, supervised classification itself is non-essential. The gap between any fine-tuned variant and vanilla isolates domain exposure.

**9-class persuasion taxonomy** (paragraph): Describe the 9 categories (0=None, 1=Rapport Building, 2=Authority Appeal, 3=Emotional Manipulation, 4=Logical Reframing, 5=Role Assignment, 6=Gradual Escalation, 7=Obfuscation, 8=Direct Request). # Task: Rewrite introduction.tex for D019 Reframe

You are rewriting the Introduction section of a paper titled "What Makes Multi-Turn Jailbreaks Detectable? Domain Exposure Bridges the Cross-Attack Gap" for EMNLP 2026.

## Critical Context: D019 Reframe

The original paper framed persuasion-aware classification as the key mechanism. An MLM control experiment **falsified** this: continued pretraining with 15% token masking (no classification labels) achieves F1=1.000 on unseen Deceptive Delight. The paper is now an **empirical findings paper**.

**New narrative arc for Introduction**:
1. Multi-turn jailbreaks distribute adversarial intent across benign turns, defeating per-turn safety filters and content-level reasoning
2. What representation properties enable cross-attack generalization? This is an open question. Vanilla encoders fail (F1=0.28 on unseen DD). LLM judges fail (GPT-5.5 F1=0.19-0.45).
3. We hypothesized persuasion-specific classification would be key. We built DisPeD with 5 variants to systematically decompose the mechanism.
4. Surprise: MLM continued pretraining without any labels achieves F1=1.0 on unseen attacks. Domain exposure, not task-specific supervision, is the mechanism.
5. Evidence hierarchy: vanilla (0.28) ≪ MLM (1.0) = scrambled (0.99) = binary (0.99) = 9-class (1.0)
6. Contributions rewritten

### Paragraph 1: Research Background (the threat)
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns. Crescendo, FITD, Deceptive Delight achieve high ASR. Each turn is individually benign; representation engineering shows attack turns occupy same embedding region as benign text (Bullwinkel 2025). Persuasion is the common mechanism (PAP, Hagendorff). Per-turn safety filters (Llama Guard, WildGuard, ShieldGemma) are fundamentally blind to distributed intent.

### Paragraph 2: The gap (what fails and why)
The natural response is to encode full conversations and track semantic drift. But vanilla semantic temporal modeling fails catastrophically on unseen attack types: F1=1.000 IID → 0.284 OOD DD. The collapse worsens with more turns (0.575 at K=1 → 0.284 at Full), consistent with each additional turn providing misleading "benign" evidence. LLM-as-judge: GPT-5.5 achieves F1=0.191-0.449, 30-47% unparseable. Content-level reasoning is insufficient. The open question: what representation properties enable cross-attack generalization?

### Paragraph 3: Our approach and the surprise finding
We hypothesized that persuasion-specific classification would be the key ingredient. We built DisPeD (Discourse-level Persuasion Detection), a two-stage framework: Stage 1 adapts DeBERTa-v3-base on jailbreak conversation text, Stage 2 aggregates via BiGRU + MLP. To test our hypothesis rigorously, we designed five Stage-1 variants that systematically decompose the mechanism: 9-class persuasion classification, binary, scrambled labels, MLM-only (15% masking, no classification), and vanilla (unfine-tuned control).

vanilla (0.28) ≪ MLM (1.0) = scrambled (0.99) = binary (0.99) = 9-class (1.0)

The 9-class persuasion taxonomy does not drive detection but provides interpretability that pure MLM cannot. This allows security analysts to inspect why conversations are flagged.
